questions.q: What are the two layer types that repeat in a standard hardware-efficient ansatz?
options: A rotation layer (parameterized single-qubit gates) and an entangling layer (two-qubit gates like CNOT)
Two separate measurement layers with no gates in between
A classical neural network layer fused directly into the quantum circuit
An encoding layer and a measurement layer only, with no trainable gates
questions.explain: The standard pattern alternates a rotation layer (independent trainable angles per qubit) with an entangling layer (fixed two-qubit gates like CNOT) to let qubits' states become correlated.

questions.q: What happens if a multi-qubit ansatz has NO entangling gates at all?
options: The circuit can still capture any multi-feature correlation, just less efficiently
The circuit becomes faster to train but otherwise identical in expressiveness
The circuit stops being a valid quantum circuit entirely
The circuit is mathematically equivalent to n separate single-qubit circuits running in parallel, unable to capture correlations between features
questions.explain: Without entangling gates, each qubit evolves independently -- the circuit can only represent functions where each output depends on each input feature in isolation, never a genuine interaction between two or more features.

questions.q: A 3-qubit ansatz has 2 layers, each applying one RY rotation per qubit (entangling gates have no trainable angle). How many total trainable parameters does it have?
questions.explain: 3 qubits x 2 layers x 1 rotation per qubit per layer = 6 trainable parameters, exactly as counted in the lesson's worked example.

questions.q: Why does the lesson say circuit depth is a cost that's fundamentally different from adding layers to a classical neural network?
options: Circuit depth has no effect whatsoever on a quantum circuit's behavior
Deeper quantum circuits always run faster than shallow ones
Each additional gate on real NISQ hardware is a new opportunity for hardware error (decoherence, gate error) to corrupt the state, not just an increase in compute time or overfitting risk
Classical neural networks never suffer from any depth-related cost
questions.explain: On real NISQ hardware, every additional gate layer adds real exposure to decoherence and gate error, which can overwhelm any benefit from extra expressiveness -- a fundamentally different cost than the compute-time/overfitting tradeoffs of classical network depth.

questions.q: A 4-qubit ansatz has 3 layers, each applying both an RY and an RZ rotation to every qubit. How many total trainable parameters does it have?
questions.explain: 4 qubits x 3 layers x 2 rotations per qubit per layer = 24 trainable parameters.
